notes: “Greater than yours” may also mean “bitter for me because of you.” Naomi speaks from her own grief.
The oath leaves its threatened punishment unnamed. The final clause can also be understood as “if even death separates you and me.”
Naomi suggests pleasantness; Mara means bitter. “The Almighty” renders Shaddai, a divine title whose origin is uncertain. “Testified against me” can also be understood as “afflicted me.”
vocabulary: Loyal care expressed in action. The same word returns in 2:20 and 3:10.
Here a settled, secure home. Related rest language returns in 3:1; Boaz will not rest in 3:18.

notes: The Hebrew’s last clause is difficult. It appears to mention a short rest in a house or field shelter; the duration and setting are not certain.
“Not to touch you” forbids interference or harm; the surrounding conversation makes Ruth’s safety a concrete concern.
The Hebrew can refer either to the LORD’s steadfast love or to Boaz’s. The living and the dead remain joined in Naomi’s blessing.
Ruth reports “young men,” while Naomi says “young women.” These differences follow the Hebrew.
vocabulary: Gather grain left behind by harvesters.
The image of refuge returns in Ruth’s request concerning Boaz’s garment in 3:9.
An ancient dry measure; the text gives an approximate amount.
A relative able to act to recover family property or protect family interests. The exact arrangement unfolds in chapter 4.

notes: The text describes uncovering Boaz’s feet and lying down. The nighttime setting and garment request carry intimate and marital implications, but the narrative does not explicitly describe intercourse.
“Wing of your garment” renders kanaph, which can mean a wing or the edge of clothing. Compare the refuge under the LORD’s wings in 2:12.
The Hebrew does not name the unit for the six measures. Its final verb is masculine: “he went,” referring to Boaz.
Literally, “Who are you, my daughter?” In context Naomi is asking about the outcome or Ruth’s changed situation; the words echo Boaz’s question in 3:9.
vocabulary: A woman of worth and capability. The same ḥayil describes Boaz in 2:1.

sections.13: A son and a restored life

notes: “So-and-so” represents an unnamed person. The narrator withholds the closer redeemer’s name.
“Is selling” can also be read “has sold.” The precise stage of the land transaction is not clear.

The traditional reading says “you acquire”; the written form says “I acquire.” The surrounding wording is also difficult, literally including “and from Ruth.” This rendering follows the traditional reading and the connection between land and marriage made in verse 10.
The women’s words associate the newborn with Naomi’s restoration. Naomi becomes his caregiver; the text does not specify a formal adoption or say that she breastfeeds him.
The Hebrew has Salmah in verse 20 and Salmon in verse 21 for the same place in the genealogy. Both forms are retained.
vocabulary: The right or action of a family redeemer; related forms recur throughout the negotiation.
The stated purpose is to preserve the dead man’s name in connection with his inherited property.
